summary: Recorded a source-only account for the newly registered investigation @joint_apply_order rather than leaving the panic unexplained or, worse, letting it drift into a defect claim. The decisive source facts now anchored: applyConfChange ends in panic(err) with a TODO asking the error be returned to the caller, so any Changer error is process-fatal rather than a rejected proposal; Changer.EnterJoint returns 'config is already joint' for a joint configuration (and LeaveJoint the mirror error for a non-joint one); and the only pre-admission guard sits in stepLeader's MsgProp path, where a conf change failing the alreadyPending / alreadyJoint && !wantsLeaveJoint / !alreadyJoint && wantsLeaveJoint checks is rewritten to a normal entry, gated on DisableConfChangeValidation and evaluated against the leader's own configuration, which Config's comment documents as best-effort with both false positives and false negatives. That fully explains the failure without implying a target defect - a lagging node applied a joint-entering change while its own tracker was still joint, which the contract treats as invalid - and it leaves the real question open: whether a permitted history with real producers and in-order application can present a node with an invalid change. Counterevidence and limits kept explicit: the harness skipped a node's whole apply step for a step at a time (coarser than real per-entry application, so it may have produced an ordering the contract never sees); the sources neither confirm nor exclude that a leader-side check correct for the leader could be wrong for a follower applying the same log with a different configuration; the panicking node's exact entry sequence and whether the propose-time check saw the change as valid are unknown; and the next step must separate the documented application duty from any target obligation, which needs a deterministic small prefix rather than more fuzzing. No experiment was requested in this short turn.
